notes.front: What is the difference between mutating and validating admission?
notes.back: Mutating admission controllers may change the object being created; validating ones may only accept or reject it.
notes.explanation: Mutating controllers run first, so a validating controller always sees the already-mutated object.
notes.example: Like an editor who can rewrite a draft, followed by a proofreader who can only approve or reject it.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Using Admission Controllers", "Admission control phases"

notes.front: What is an admission webhook?
notes.back: An HTTP callback (MutatingAdmissionWebhook or ValidatingAdmissionWebhook) that runs your own custom admission logic.
notes.explanation: It is one of the extension points that let organisations plug custom policy checks into the built-in admission chain.
notes.example: Like inviting an outside inspector to sign off on a request before it proceeds.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Using Admission Controllers", "Admission control extension points"

notes.front: What is a ValidatingAdmissionPolicy (VAP)?
notes.back: A declarative, in-process alternative to validating admission webhooks, written in CEL; stable since v1.30.
notes.explanation: Because it runs inside the API server, it avoids the network round trip and availability risk of an external webhook.
notes.example: Like a rule baked directly into the checkpoint, rather than phoning an outside office for every decision.

notes.front: What is MutatingAdmissionPolicy?
notes.back: The declarative, in-process mutating counterpart to ValidatingAdmissionPolicy; enabled when its feature gate and API version are both on.
notes.explanation: It can apply mutations either as a server-side-apply merge or as a JSON patch, without an external webhook.
notes.example: Like the editor from before, but now working from a fixed rulebook instead of freehand judgement.

notes.front: What is the Common Expression Language (CEL)?
notes.back: The expression language behind Kubernetes' newer declarative policy features, such as ValidatingAdmissionPolicy.
notes.explanation: CEL expressions are evaluated in-process, which is what lets these policies avoid an external webhook call.
notes.example: Like a small, purpose-built formula language, rather than a full programming language, for writing pass/fail rules.

notes.front: What are default admission plugins?
notes.back: The admission plugins enabled by default, including CertificateApproval, LimitRanger, PodSecurity, ResourceQuota, ServiceAccount, ValidatingAdmissionPolicy and the webhook plugins.
notes.explanation: A cluster missing the recommended default set is considered an incomplete server that won't support all expected features.
notes.example: Like the standard checks a building already runs at every entrance, before any custom rule is added.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Using Admission Controllers", "Which plugins are enabled by default?"

notes.front: What does the NodeRestriction admission plugin limit?
notes.back: It limits a kubelet (in the system:nodes group) to modifying only its own Node object and Pods bound to it.
notes.explanation: It also blocks kubelets from removing taints on their Node, or setting labels under the reserved node-restriction.kubernetes.io/ prefix.
notes.example: Like a badge that only opens the one office assigned to its holder, not the whole floor.

notes.front: What does the AlwaysPullImages admission plugin do?
notes.back: It forces every new Pod's imagePullPolicy to Always, so private images can only be used by clients holding valid pull credentials.
notes.explanation: Without it, once an image is cached on a node, any Pod scheduled there could reuse it by name, bypassing that check.
notes.example: Like re-checking ID at the door every time, rather than trusting whoever is already inside.

notes.front: What does the ImagePolicyWebhook admission plugin do?
notes.back: It asks an external webhook whether a Pod's images are allowed, before the Pod is admitted.
notes.explanation: It is the admission-time hook that lets organisations enforce their own image-vetting policy, such as requiring signed images.
notes.example: Like a delivery gate that phones the warehouse to check each package is on the approved list.

notes.front: What does the DenyServiceExternalIPs admission plugin do?
notes.back: It rejects any new use of the Service externalIPs field, which can be used to intercept traffic. The plugin itself is off by default.
notes.explanation: Existing uses are left alone, but no new Service can start using externalIPs once this plugin is enabled.
notes.example: Like closing a rarely used, risky side door for new traffic while leaving existing traffic through it alone.

notes.front: What does the CertificateSubjectRestriction admission plugin do?
notes.back: It rejects any CertificateSigningRequest that requests the group system:masters, when the signer is kubernetes.io/kube-apiserver-client.
notes.explanation: It closes off a certificate-issuing route to the group that bypasses RBAC and webhook authorizers entirely.
notes.example: Like refusing to print any ID card that claims to be a master key, no matter who requests it.

notes.front: What do PodNodeSelector and PodTolerationRestriction do?
notes.back: PodNodeSelector forces node selectors per namespace; PodTolerationRestriction limits which tolerations a namespace's Pods may use.
notes.explanation: Both are ways to keep workloads in one namespace confined to a chosen set of nodes.
notes.example: Like assigning each department to specific floors, and restricting which restricted areas their badges can bypass.

notes.front: What does the EventRateLimit admission plugin do?
notes.back: It mitigates the API server being flooded by Event creation requests, by rate-limiting per server, namespace, user, or source and object.
notes.explanation: It is an alpha, disabled-by-default plugin, so it needs explicit configuration to protect against this kind of overload.
notes.example: Like a turnstile that caps how many times per minute any one person can swipe through.

notes.front: What is a policy engine, in the Kubernetes context?
notes.back: A tool that evaluates policy as code, typically deployed as an admission webhook, such as Gatekeeper, Kyverno or Kubewarden.
notes.explanation: Policy engines let teams write and manage cluster-wide rules as ordinary, reviewable code rather than scattered manual checks.
notes.example: Like a rulebook a checkpoint consults automatically, instead of a guard improvising each decision.

notes.front: What is Open Policy Agent (OPA)?
notes.back: A CNCF-graduated, general-purpose policy engine with a declarative policy language (Rego), used across microservices, Kubernetes and CI/CD.
notes.explanation: OPA decouples the policy decision from how it is enforced: software queries OPA and supplies structured data as input.
notes.example: Like a shared rules office any system can ask "is this allowed?", instead of each system writing its own rules.

notes.front: What is Gatekeeper?
notes.back: A validating and mutating admission webhook that enforces CRD-based policies executed by OPA, plus an audit function for existing violations.
notes.explanation: Its ConstraintTemplate and Constraint CRDs let policies be instantiated as native Kubernetes objects, unlike raw OPA alone.
notes.example: Like OPA's rules office, but now wired directly into the checkpoint with native paperwork the cluster understands.

notes.front: What is Kyverno?
notes.back: A cloud native policy engine, originally built for Kubernetes, whose policies are written as declarative YAML and CEL Kubernetes resources.
notes.explanation: Unlike Gatekeeper, it needs no separate policy language: its policies use the same YAML and CEL Kubernetes users already know.
notes.example: Like writing checkpoint rules in the same paperwork format the rest of the building already uses.

notes.front: What is Kubewarden?
notes.back: A third-party policy engine listed in the Kubernetes documentation as an alternative to the built-in Pod Security Standards enforcement.
notes.explanation: It's named alongside Kyverno and OPA Gatekeeper as another way to enforce policy through admission control.
notes.example: Like a third vendor offering the same kind of rules office as OPA or Kyverno.

notes.front: In what order do the two admission phases run?
notes.back: Mutating admission controllers run first, then validating ones; if either phase rejects the request, the whole request fails immediately.
notes.explanation: This ordering means validating controllers always see the object after every mutation has already been applied.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Using Admission Controllers", "Admission control phases"

notes.front: Can an admission controller block a get, watch or list request?
notes.back: No. Admission controllers only apply to requests that create, delete or modify objects; reads bypass admission entirely.
notes.explanation: This is why a validating webhook can never stop kubectl get secrets from returning data it would otherwise reject on write.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Using Admission Controllers", "What are they?"

notes.front: Do matching mutating webhooks run serially or in parallel, and why does it matter?
notes.back: Serially, each able to modify the object. A change re-runs built-in mutating plugins, and webhooks opted in with reinvocationPolicy: IfNeeded.
notes.explanation: Validating webhooks, by contrast, run in parallel and cannot mutate the object.

notes.front: Why must a webhook with side effects, such as decrementing quota, have its own reconciliation system?
notes.back: Because it is not guaranteed that later admission controllers will still let the overall request finish.
notes.explanation: A side effect made early on can be left orphaned if a later controller rejects the request.

notes.front: What flags enable and disable admission plugins on the API server?
notes.back: --enable-admission-plugins to add plugins, --disable-admission-plugins to remove them, even ones enabled by default.
notes.explanation: Both take a comma-delimited list, so multiple plugins can be adjusted in a single flag.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Using Admission Controllers", "How do I turn on/off an admission controller?"

notes.front: Is NodeRestriction among the admission plugins enabled by default?
notes.back: No. It must be explicitly enabled, unlike ValidatingAdmissionPolicy, ServiceAccount and PodSecurity.
notes.explanation: Leaving it out unintentionally removes one of the boundaries between a kubelet and the rest of the cluster's API objects.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Using Admission Controllers", "Which plugins are enabled by default?"

notes.front: What language do ValidatingAdmissionPolicy rules use to declare validation logic?
notes.back: CEL, the Common Expression Language.
notes.explanation: CEL expressions run inside the API server, avoiding the network call and availability risk of a validating webhook.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Validating Admission Policy", "What is Validating Admission Policy?"

notes.front: A cluster wants to reject any Pod whose image isn't cryptographically signed, calling out to an external decision service. Which built-in admission plugin fits directly?
notes.back: ImagePolicyWebhook, which asks an external webhook whether a Pod's images are allowed.
notes.explanation: AlwaysPullImages forces images to be freshly pulled, but it doesn't itself check signatures; that decision belongs to ImagePolicyWebhook.

notes.front: In a multi-tenant cluster, one tenant's Pod pulled a private image that is now cached on a node. Without AlwaysPullImages, what could another tenant's Pod do?
notes.back: Reuse that cached image by name on the same node, without any authorization check against it.
notes.explanation: AlwaysPullImages closes this gap by forcing a fresh pull, which re-triggers the credential check, for every Pod.

notes.front: A compromised kubelet, authenticated as system:node:worker-1, tries to modify a Pod scheduled on a different node. Does NodeRestriction allow this?
notes.back: No. NodeRestriction only lets a kubelet modify Pods bound to its own Node object.
notes.explanation: This limits the blast radius of a single compromised node to the workloads actually running on it.

notes.front: A user submits a CertificateSigningRequest with organization field system:masters, signed by kubernetes.io/kube-apiserver-client. Is it accepted?
notes.back: No, if CertificateSubjectRestriction is enabled; it explicitly rejects requests for that group under that signer.
notes.explanation: Without this plugin, a certificate could grant its holder the same unrestricted access as manual system:masters membership.

notes.front: A platform team wants to write cluster policies entirely as native Kubernetes YAML resources, using CEL, with no separate policy language to learn. Which policy engine best fits this?
notes.back: Kyverno, whose policies are declarative Kubernetes resources written in YAML and CEL.
notes.explanation: OPA Gatekeeper, by contrast, uses Rego, a separate policy language, inside its ConstraintTemplate objects.

notes.front: A team wants a simple, self-contained admission rule that never depends on an external service being reachable. Should they reach for a validating webhook or a ValidatingAdmissionPolicy?
notes.back: A ValidatingAdmissionPolicy, since it runs its CEL expressions inside the API server, with no external HTTP dependency.
notes.explanation: A validating webhook's decision depends on a remote service actually responding; a CEL policy has no such dependency.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Validating Admission Policy", "What is Validating Admission Policy?"

notes.front: What is the difference between a validating admission webhook and a ValidatingAdmissionPolicy?
notes.back: A webhook makes an external HTTP call for a decision; a ValidatingAdmissionPolicy evaluates CEL expressions inside the API server itself.
notes.explanation: The in-process policy avoids the network dependency and latency a webhook always carries.
notes.contrast: A webhook asks an outside service; a policy decides on its own.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Using Admission Controllers", "Admission control extension points"

notes.front: What is the difference between mutating and validating admission controllers?
notes.back: Mutating controllers may rewrite the incoming object; validating controllers can only accept or reject it as it stands.
notes.explanation: Mutating controllers always run first, so their changes are what validating controllers actually check.
notes.contrast: One edits the request; the other only judges it.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Using Admission Controllers", "Admission control phases"

notes.front: What is the difference between OPA and Gatekeeper?
notes.back: OPA is a general-purpose policy engine usable anywhere; Gatekeeper wraps it as a Kubernetes admission webhook, with native CRD policies and an audit function.
notes.explanation: Gatekeeper adds Kubernetes-native ConstraintTemplate and Constraint objects on top of what plain OPA provides.
notes.contrast: OPA is the engine; Gatekeeper is its Kubernetes-shaped packaging.
notes.source: OPA Gatekeeper documentation, "Introduction", "How is Gatekeeper different from OPA?"

notes.front: Is ImagePolicyWebhook a validating or mutating plugin, and is it on by default?
notes.back: Validating only, and it is disabled by default; it must be explicitly enabled and configured.
notes.explanation: Being validating-only, it can reject a Pod's images but never alter what the Pod requests.

notes.front: What format does ImagePolicyWebhook's configuration file use to describe its backend, and what else can it set?
notes.back: A kubeconfig-style file naming the backend service, plus a cache time in seconds for how long an approval is trusted.
notes.explanation: Reusing the kubeconfig format keeps its configuration consistent with other webhook-based extension points.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Using Admission Controllers", "Configuration file format"

notes.front: What are the four special admission control extension points?
notes.back: MutatingAdmissionWebhook, MutatingAdmissionPolicy, ValidatingAdmissionWebhook, and ValidatingAdmissionPolicy.
notes.explanation: The webhook pair calls out to external HTTP services; the policy pair evaluates CEL in-process instead.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Using Admission Controllers", "Admission control extension points"

notes.front: What are the four bucket types EventRateLimit can apply its limits by?
notes.back: Server (one shared bucket for all Events), Namespace, User, and SourceAndObject.
notes.explanation: Choosing the right bucket type controls whose Event traffic is throttled together versus separately.

notes.front: What is OPA's declarative policy language called?
notes.back: Rego, the high-level language OPA uses to write policy as code.
notes.explanation: Rego is what separates OPA's own policies from Kyverno's, which instead uses ordinary YAML and CEL.

notes.front: What two policy areas does Gatekeeper support, and which resources configure each?
notes.back: Validation, using ConstraintTemplate and Constraint resources, and mutation, using AssignMetadata, Assign, ModifySet and AssignImage.
notes.explanation: Validation can only judge a resource; mutation can actually change it during admission, before validation runs.

notes.front: What does Gatekeeper's audit functionality do that admission alone can't?
notes.back: It lets administrators see which already-existing resources currently violate a given policy, not just block new violations at admission time.
notes.explanation: This catches resources that predate a policy, or that changed through a route admission never saw.

notes.front: What can a Kyverno policy do to a Kubernetes resource?
notes.back: Validate, mutate, generate, or cleanup (remove) it.
notes.explanation: This is broader than a typical validating or mutating webhook alone, which usually covers only one or two of these actions.

notes.front: Is AlwaysPullImages a mutating or a validating admission plugin?
notes.back: Both: it mutates the Pod's imagePullPolicy to Always, and enforces that change so pulls always require valid credentials.
notes.explanation: It is one of the plugins that acts in both phases; it is not enabled by default.

notes.front: Which label prefixes does NodeRestriction block a kubelet from setting on its own Node object?
notes.back: node-restriction.kubernetes.io/ and node-role.kubernetes.io/.
notes.explanation: The first is reserved for administrator workload-isolation labels; the second stops an unprivileged node self-declaring a cluster role.

notes.front: A compromised kubelet tries to label its own Node object node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane: "true", hoping to claim control-plane status. Does NodeRestriction allow this?
notes.back: No. Labels under the node-role.kubernetes.io/ prefix are forbidden for a kubelet to set on itself.
notes.explanation: This stops a compromised worker node from self-promoting into a more trusted role through its own Node labels.

notes.front: A cluster wants noisy Event creation in one tenant's namespace to never crowd out another tenant's Events. Which EventRateLimit bucket type fits?
notes.back: Namespace, which gives each namespace its own dedicated bucket.
notes.explanation: The Server type would instead share one bucket across the whole cluster, letting one namespace still starve the rest.

notes.front: A platform team wants to add a default label to every new Pod declaratively, in-process, without standing up an external webhook service. Which admission mechanism fits?
notes.back: MutatingAdmissionPolicy, the declarative, in-process mutating counterpart to ValidatingAdmissionPolicy.
notes.explanation: It applies its mutation as a server-side-apply merge or a JSON patch, entirely inside the API server.

notes.front: A security team inherits a cluster and wants to find every currently running resource that would violate a new policy, not just block future ones. Which Gatekeeper feature covers this?
notes.back: Gatekeeper's audit functionality, which checks existing resources against a policy independently of admission.
notes.explanation: A validating webhook or admission policy alone only ever sees new or updated requests, never resources already sitting in the cluster.

notes.front: A team wants a single policy engine that can also generate companion resources and clean up stale ones, not just validate or mutate. Which engine's documented feature set covers this directly?
notes.back: Kyverno, whose policies can validate, mutate, generate or cleanup (remove) any Kubernetes resource.
notes.explanation: This is a broader remit than a typical admission webhook, which usually only validates or mutates the one incoming request.

notes.front: Is AlwaysPullImages purely a validating admission plugin?
notes.back: No. It's both mutating (it forces imagePullPolicy to Always) and validating (that setting then requires valid pull credentials).
notes.explanation: Confusing it for validating-only misses that it actively changes the Pod spec before any check runs.

notes.front: Is ValidatingAdmissionWebhook the only way to extend admission control beyond the built-in plugins?
notes.back: No. There are four extension points: MutatingAdmissionWebhook, MutatingAdmissionPolicy, ValidatingAdmissionWebhook and ValidatingAdmissionPolicy.
notes.explanation: The two policy-based extension points avoid needing an external webhook service at all.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Using Admission Controllers", "Admission control extension points"

notes.front: What is the difference between the policy languages OPA and Kyverno use?
notes.back: OPA (and Gatekeeper) use Rego, a purpose-built policy language; Kyverno uses ordinary YAML with CEL expressions.
notes.explanation: This is a large part of Kyverno's pitch: no new language to learn on top of what Kubernetes users already write.
notes.contrast: Rego is a language built specifically for policy; CEL in Kyverno rides on YAML that already looks like Kubernetes.
notes.source: Open Policy Agent documentation and Kyverno documentation, "Introduction"

notes.front: A team configuring ImagePolicyWebhook's backend connection wants to reuse a format they already know from other Kubernetes webhook configs. Which format does its configuration file use?
notes.back: The kubeconfig file format, naming the backend service and a cache duration for approvals.
notes.explanation: This is the same pattern webhook token authentication and webhook authorization also use for their remote service configuration.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Using Admission Controllers", "Configuration file format"

notes.front: An admission webhook needs to inject a sidecar container into every new Pod, then reject any Pod that still fails policy afterwards. Which two phases does this need?
notes.back: Mutating admission, to inject the sidecar, followed by validating admission, to reject Pods that still fail the check.
notes.explanation: Mutating controllers always run before validating ones, so validation sees the already-mutated object.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Using Admission Controllers", "Admission control phases"

notes.front: A platform team wants one shared policy engine that microservices, CI/CD pipelines and Kubernetes admission can all query the same way. Which general-purpose engine fits?
notes.back: Open Policy Agent (OPA): a CNCF-graduated engine used across microservices, Kubernetes and CI/CD, not tied to Kubernetes admission alone.
notes.explanation: OPA decouples the policy decision from how it's enforced, which is what lets one engine serve several different systems.
